name: What would you preregister?
note: Before prompting, you commit the contract the AI's output must satisfy. Pick the thing most worth committing first — the one that guards the failure the happy path hides.

items.prompt: Task: parse a CSV file into records. What's the most valuable invariant to preregister before prompting?
candidates: Every output record has exactly the header's field count, and malformed rows are surfaced, not silently dropped — the failure the AI's happy-path parser is most likely to paper over
The function should be named parse_csv
It should use the standard library csv module
It should finish in under one second
items.correct: Every output record has exactly the header's field count, and malformed rows are surfaced, not silently dropped — the failure the AI's happy-path parser is most likely to paper over
items.explanation: Invariants should target the silent-failure surface (dropped or merged rows on ragged input), which is exactly what a fluent happy-path implementation tends to skip. Naming, module choice, and speed are details, not the contract.
items.principle: Preregister the invariant that guards the failure the happy path hides.

items.prompt: Task: write a sync that pushes local changes to a server. What's the defining invariant to commit first?
candidates: Idempotence: running the sync twice with no new local changes produces no second write — the property that separates a safe sync from one that duplicates data
It should print 'done' when it finishes
It should be implemented as a single function
It should use HTTPS for the requests
items.correct: Idempotence: running the sync twice with no new local changes produces no second write — the property that separates a safe sync from one that duplicates data
items.explanation: Idempotence is the correctness property that defines a sync. Committing it before prompting steers the AI toward a safe design and hands you the test that actually matters; transport and structure are secondary.
items.principle: For anything that writes, idempotence is the invariant worth committing first.

items.prompt: You wrote a test after seeing the AI's output, and it passed. Is that verification?
candidates: Not on its own — a test written after seeing the code tends to encode what the code already does; the same test written from the spec, before prompting, would also have constrained the cases the code missed
Yes — a passing test is a passing test regardless of when it was written
No — tests are never useful for AI-generated code
Yes, as long as you have at least five of them
items.correct: Not on its own — a test written after seeing the code tends to encode what the code already does; the same test written from the spec, before prompting, would also have constrained the cases the code missed
items.explanation: Timing changes what a test measures. A post-hoc test ratifies the AI's choices; a preregistered test constrains them. Write the standard from the spec, before the output exists — that's what makes 'green' mean something.
items.principle: A test's value depends on whether the code could bias it — write it before the code exists.
